doctrines.question: Do the miraculous spiritual gifts described in the New Testament continue in the church today?
doctrines.framing: Every tradition agrees that the New Testament describes tongues, prophecy, healing and other miraculous gifts operating in the apostolic church. The disagreement is over whether those gifts were tied to the foundational apostolic era and its accompanying sign of Scripture-authenticating revelation, or continue as an ordinary part of the Spirit's work in the church until Christ returns.
doctrines.tier_note: Thomas's own map places continuationism at the second tier: it shapes how a congregation worships and what it expects of the Spirit, without dividing on the gospel itself.

open.todo: Work out whether 'the perfect' in 1 Corinthians 13:10 refers to the completed canon, the return of Christ, or something else, and decide whether Acts' pattern of ongoing tongues and prophecy is descriptive of an apostolic season or a standing norm.

positions.label: Cessationist
positions.hold: The revelatory and sign gifts, including tongues, prophecy and the working of miracles as attesting apostolic ministry, ceased with the apostolic era and the completion of the New Testament canon.
positions.why: The sign gifts served to authenticate the apostles' foundational message before Scripture was complete, and the New Testament itself anticipates their passing once what is perfect, understood as the completed revelation, has come.
positions.vs: Continuing the full range of New Testament spiritual gifts as an ordinary part of church life today.

held_by.note: Not confessionally required by the Westminster Standards themselves, but the predominant position among Reformed and Presbyterian bodies since the modern cessationist-continuationist debate emerged.
Widely but not universally held; the Baptist Faith and Message does not itself settle the question.
held_by.citation: John MacArthur, Charismatic Chaos (1992), representative of a major strand of Baptist cessationism

positions.learn_detail: Cessationism is a position about the sign and revelatory gifts specifically; cessationists typically still affirm that God heals and answers prayer, distinguishing ordinary providence from the apostolic sign gifts.

positions.label: Continuationist
positions.hold: The spiritual gifts described in 1 Corinthians 12, including tongues, prophecy and healing, continue to be given by the Holy Spirit to the church today and are to be earnestly desired.
positions.why: Paul commands the Corinthian church to desire spiritual gifts and gives no indication that they would cease before Christ's return, and 'the perfect' of 1 Corinthians 13:10 is most naturally the eschaton rather than the closing of the canon.
positions.vs: Restricting the sign and revelatory gifts to the apostolic era before the completion of the New Testament canon.

held_by.citation: Assemblies of God, Statement of Fundamental Truths, Article 7-8
International Network of Churches, Statement of Faith

held_by.note: Practice varies widely; many independent evangelical congregations are charismatic in expectation without a formal confessional statement on the gifts.
Affirmed through the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, recognised by Rome, alongside a broader church that does not emphasise the gifts.
Held within the charismatic wing of the Communion; not a position the Articles themselves address.
held_by.citation: Church of England, House of Bishops, statements recognising charismatic renewal within the Communion

positions.learn_detail: Continuationists divide further on how the gifts are exercised in practice, from classical Pentecostal expectation of tongues as initial evidence of Spirit baptism to a lighter charismatic openness within otherwise traditional worship.

sources.label: Assemblies of God Statement of Fundamental Truths

doctrines.learn_note: The debate is often framed as for-or-against the miraculous as such; both positions affirm that God still heals and answers prayer. The actual dispute is narrower: whether the New Testament sign and revelatory gifts specifically continue.
